fast.topic:
Week 4 traces Nigeria's constitutional development through four constitutions.

It starts with Lord Lugard's advisory Nigerian Council of 1914: 36 members, six unofficial.

Sir Hugh Clifford took over in 1919 and produced Nigeria's first written constitution in 1922. It set up three units: Lagos Colony, Southern Provinces, Northern Provinces. It gave a 45-member legislative council of 26 official Europeans, 15 nominated members and 4 elected Nigerians (3 Lagos, 1 Calabar). It brought in the elective principle, and Cameroon joining Nigeria. Against that: the Governor's veto, no local input and no Northern representation.

Then the interim governors. Sir Graham Thompson (1926). Sir Donald Cameron (1930-1936), who abolished the Lieutenant Governor's office and the provincial court and introduced separation of powers. Bernard Bourdillon (1935).

Sir Arthur Richards' constitution of 1947-1951 introduced regionalism. Three regional Houses of Assembly, a bicameral North, and 28 Nigerians of 45 council members with 4 elected. Two Nigerians on the Executive Council in 1949.

Macpherson was Governor from 1948 and consulted widely. In 1951 he created the 136-member House of Representatives and the Council of Ministers, with the Governor as Prime Minister and twelve ministers. It fell within three years to Enahoro's motion for independence.

Sir Oliver Lyttleton, a Colonial Secretary rather than a Governor, then introduced federalism in 1954. With it came regional Premiers, a regionalised judiciary, Lagos as Federal Capital Territory and revenue allocation by derivation.

The second strand covers the parties.

Herbert Macaulay's NNDP: 1923, the Lagos Daily News, winning all three Lagos seats in 1923, 1928 and 1933.

The Nigeria Youth Movement: 1935, Ernest Ikoli and Samuel Akisanya, the Daily Service. It took all elective seats from the NNDP in 1938 and was destroyed by internal disputes in 1944.

The NCNC: August 1944, Macaulay as first President and Nnamdi Azikiwe as first General Secretary, the West African Pilot, and the protest delegation against the 1946 constitution.

The Action Group: Ibadan, 1951, from Egbe Omo Oduduwa of 1945, founded by Awolowo, the Ooni and Ajasin.

The NPC: 1951, from Jam'iyyar Mutanen Arewa, founded by Ahmadu Bello the Sardauna of Sokoto, Tafawa Balewa, Yahaya Gusau and Aminu Kano.

Then the four criticisms of Nigerian parties: ethnocentrism, lack of ideology, a weakened centre, and ethnic interest over national interest.

The third strand is the weekly summary on the Amalgamation of 1914 that united Northern and Southern Nigeria.

Its two schools of thought: that it merely formalised pre-existing inter-group relations, or that it created a deeply divided nation.

Then the views of Dudley, Olusanya, E. Osaghae, Claude Ake and Lord Lugard on the civil war, national integration, and the failure of post-independence leaders to address colonial legacies.

fast.topic:
This week covers paragraph construction and punctuation.

The paragraph deck defines a paragraph as an individual unit of thought within a written composition.

It names the four components of a good paragraph: unity, coherence, the topic sentence, and one idea at a time. Unity is a single central theme with no digression. Coherence is ideas ordered logically and joined by cohesive links such as conjunctions and pronouns.

It distinguishes the topic sentence, which states the main idea and usually opens the paragraph, from supporting sentences or supporting details. The worked example is the Body Positivity specimen. It states the rule that five paragraphs require five topic sentences.

It then sorts transition words into categories: addition, contrast, comparison, cause and effect, emphasis, sequence or order, illustration or example, conclusion or summary, time, and clarification.

The punctuation deck sets out four uses of punctuation: changing the meaning, emphasising a point, conveying nuance, and clarifying ambiguity. The illustrations are Let's eat, Grandma and I like cooking, my family, and pets.

It then covers each mark with its rule and examples.

The period, comma, semicolon, colon, apostrophe, quotation marks, question mark, exclamation point, hyphen. The dash, with the em dash and en dash distinguished. The ellipsis, parentheses, brackets, slash, and ampersand.

The week's summary strand adds writing strategies, treated as analogous to programming languages. It lists persuasion, narration, description, exposition, comparison, contrast, cause and effect, problem-solution, definition, chronological order, and process analysis.

It also adds tone and style, audience awareness, editing and revision, and the four sentence types: declarative, interrogative, imperative, and exclamatory.

deep.topic:
Week 4 of Elementary Mathematics II worked as problems: taking numbers off graphs and out of formulas.

Reading lim as x approaches c from the left, from the right, the two-sided limit, and the value f(c), from a described graph.

Classifying the point as removable, jump or infinite from the pair of one-sided limits.

The algebraic cases the deck uses: lim(x→3) of 2x+1 read off a line of slope 2 and intercept 1; lim(x→1) of (x²−1)/(x−1) by factoring and cancelling; and one-sided limits of |x| and |x|/x at 0.

Then choosing a constant that makes a piecewise function continuous at its joining point.

Also diagnosing wrong routes. In particular, treating the indeterminate form 0/0 as proof that a limit does not exist, and checking a classification against the graph before quoting it.

fast.topic:
This week's practical is the experimental verification of Kirchhoff's Current Law.

It is the first of Kirchhoff's two circuit laws. It follows from conservation of electric charge. It states that the sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of those leaving it.

The circuit is built on a breadboard from five variable resistors, two DC power supplies and three ammeters. R1 to R5 are set to 10, 1, 2.5, 7 and 5 kilohms. Both supplies are put on the 50 V maximum-output range and their emfs dialled to 9 V.

The three branch currents I1, I2 and I3 at the node are then recorded. The run is repeated with the emf raised in regular 3 V steps to 12 V and 15 V.

Verification is done by computing I3 as I1 plus I2 for each row. The sign convention is kept: currents entering the node are positive, those leaving are negative. That computed value is then compared with the current the third ammeter actually measured.

The measured I2 is negative throughout, which simply means that branch carries current away from the junction. In every row the algebraic sum reproduces the measured I3 exactly.

The conclusion is that no charge accumulates at the junction, and that KCL holds independently of the emf applied. So the node equation minus I1 minus I2 plus I3 equals zero is confirmed by experiment.

checks.topic:
Week 4 of Elementary Mathematics II, taken conceptually.

What the objects in a limit statement actually are, and why each continuity criterion is there.

The three-condition definition of continuity at a point c: f(c) defined, lim as x approaches c exists, and the two are equal.

One-sided limits, and the existence criterion that the left and right limits must agree on one finite real number.

What an open circle and a shaded dot each encode on a graph.

Why 'limit equals infinity' is a description of failure rather than a value.

The four types of discontinuity (removable, jump, infinite, essential) as names for which criterion fails and in what way.

Why a removable one can be repaired by redefining a single point, and a jump or infinite one cannot.

No computation is required. Every question asks what breaks without a given condition.

questions.q: For x < 1 a curve rises and ends in an open circle at (1, 5). For x > 1 the curve begins at a solid dot at (1, 2) and continues to the right. Find lim(x→1⁻) f(x).
questions.concept: Left-hand limit from a described graph
questions.why:
The left-hand limit is the height the curve runs into as x approaches 1 from values below 1. The left branch runs into the open circle at height 5, and an open circle still shows the approach height, so lim(x→1⁻) f(x) = 5.

2 is the right-hand limit and also f(1), read from the solid dot; DNE is the two-sided limit, which fails because 5 ≠ 2, but the question asks for one side only; 1 is the x-value, not a height.

questions.q: At x = 3 both branches of a curve run into an open circle at (3, 4). A solid dot sits at (3, −1). State f(3).
questions.concept: Function value from a shaded dot
questions.why:
The value f(3) is the height of the solid (shaded) dot on the line x = 3, so f(3) = −1. The open circle marks a height the curve approaches but does not take.

4 is lim(x→3) f(x), the approach height, not the value; 'undefined' would be right only if there were no solid dot at all; 3 is the input, not the output.

questions.q: g(x) = |x|. Find lim(x→0⁻) g(x) and g(0).
questions.concept: One-sided limit of the absolute value at its corner
questions.why:
For x < 0, |x| = −x, so as x → 0⁻ the heights are 0.5, 0.1, 0.01, … → 0. So lim(x→0⁻) |x| = 0, and g(0) = |0| = 0. The V has a sharp corner at the origin but no break, so the function is continuous there.

'DNE and 0' treats the corner as a break; '−1 and 1' confuses |x| with |x|/x, whose sides are −1 and 1; '0 and undefined' forgets that |0| = 0 is a perfectly good value.

questions.q: lim(x→5⁻) f(x) = 2, lim(x→5⁺) f(x) = −2 and f(5) = 2. Find lim(x→5) f(x).
questions.concept: Existence of a two-sided limit from the one-sided limits
questions.why:
A two-sided limit exists only when the left and right limits agree on one finite number. Here 2 ≠ −2, so lim(x→5) f(x) = DNE.

2 quotes the left limit or the value f(5), neither of which decides the two-sided limit; −2 quotes the right limit only; 0 averages the two sides, which is never how a limit is found.

questions.concept: Estimating a limit from a table of values
questions.why:
From the left the heights 5.8, 5.98, 5.998 climb toward 6; from the right the heights 6.2, 6.02, 6.002 fall toward 6. Both sides settle on the same number, so lim(x→3) f(x) = 6.

3 is the input being approached, not the output; 5.998 is the last entry in the table, not the number the entries are heading for; DNE wrongly reads 5.998 ≠ 6.002 as the two sides disagreeing, when both are closing in on 6.

questions.q: The graph of f(x) = 3x + 5 is an unbroken straight line. Find lim(x→−2) f(x).
questions.concept: Limit of a linear function read from its graph
questions.why:
The line has slope 3 and y-intercept 5 and has no hole, jump or break at x = −2, so both sides run into the height of the line there: 3(−2) + 5 = −6 + 5 = −1.

5 is the y-intercept, where the line meets the y-axis, not its height at x = −2; 3 is the slope; 11 drops the sign of −2 and computes 3(2) + 5.

questions.q: f(x) = x + 3 for every x ≠ 2, and f(2) = 9. Find lim(x→2) f(x) and say whether f is continuous at x = 2.
questions.concept: Continuity when the function value is off the curve
questions.why:
The limit uses only x near 2, never x = 2 itself, so lim(x→2) f(x) = 2 + 3 = 5. But f(2) = 9 ≠ 5, so the third continuity condition fails and f is not continuous at 2 (a removable discontinuity: a hole at (2, 5) with a stray dot at (2, 9)).

'9; continuous' lets the value f(2) dictate the limit; '5; continuous' finds the limit but forgets to compare it with f(2); 'DNE' treats the misplaced dot as if it broke the limit, which depends only on the approach from both sides.

questions.q: lim(x→a⁻) f(x) = 1 and lim(x→a⁺) f(x) = 4. A student defines f(a) = 4 so that f becomes continuous at a. Why does this fail?
options: f(a) should be 1, the left-hand value
f(a) should be 2.5, the average of 1 and 4
lim(x→a) f(x) still does not exist
It does not fail; f is now continuous at a
questions.concept: Why a jump discontinuity cannot be repaired
questions.why:
Continuity needs lim(x→a) f(x) to exist and to equal f(a). The two-sided limit fails because the sides disagree (1 ≠ 4), and no choice of f(a) changes what the sides approach. A jump is a failure of the second condition, so redefining one point cannot fix it.

Choosing 1 or 2.5 for f(a) still leaves the one-sided limits at 1 and 4; 'now continuous' matches f(a) to one side only, but the other side still disagrees.

questions.q: For x < −1 a curve falls and ends in an open circle at (−1, 2). For x > −1 the curve starts at a solid dot at (−1, 5) and continues upward. Give lim(x→−1⁻) f(x), lim(x→−1⁺) f(x), lim(x→−1) f(x), f(−1) and the type of discontinuity.
questions.concept: Reading all four quantities from a graph
questions.why:
The left branch runs into height 2, so lim(x→−1⁻) f(x) = 2; an open circle still records the height being approached. The right branch starts at height 5, so lim(x→−1⁺) f(x) = 5. The two sides disagree, so lim(x→−1) f(x) is DNE, while the solid dot fixes the value f(−1) = 5. Two finite but unequal one-sided limits is exactly a jump discontinuity.

Reading f(−1) off the open circle gives 2, calling the two-sided limit 5 takes one side for both, and 'removable' would need the two sides to agree.

questions.q: f(x) = (x² − x − 6)/(x − 3). Find lim(x→3) f(x), say whether f(3) is defined, and name the type of discontinuity at x = 3.
options: 5, f(3) = 5, so f is continuous there
questions.concept: Removable discontinuity of a rational function
questions.why:
Substituting 3 gives (9 − 3 − 6)/0 = 0/0, which is a signal to factor rather than an answer. Since x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2), for every x ≠ 3 the function equals x + 2, so lim(x→3) f(x) = 5 from both sides, while f(3) itself is undefined because the denominator vanishes. A limit that exists at a point where the function does not is the removable case: the line y = x + 2 with a hole at (3, 5).

'DNE because 0/0' misreads the indeterminate form, 0 reads the numerator alone, and f(3) = 5 forgets that cancelling does not restore the point.

questions.q: f(x) = x² for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = 2 − x for x > 1. Give f(1), the left limit and the right limit at x = 1, and say whether f is continuous there.
options: f(1) = 1, left 1, right 1; not continuous, since the two rules differ
questions.concept: Continuity of a piecewise function at its join
questions.why:
Because 1 ≤ 1, the value comes from the first piece: f(1) = 1² = 1, so f is defined there. From the left, lim x² = 1; from the right, lim (2 − x) = 2 − 1 = 1, so the two sides agree and lim(x→1) f(x) = 1 exists. That limit equals f(1), so all three conditions hold and f is continuous at x = 1.

A right limit of 2 substitutes into 2 − x carelessly, f(1) = 2 uses the wrong piece, and the last option confuses different formulas with a genuine break.

questions.q: lim(x→c) f(x) exists only when the two one-sided limits agree on the same finite real number. Which pair names the two ways that can fail?
options: f(c) is undefined, or f(c) differs from the limit
The curve has a corner at c, or f is not differentiable at c
The one-sided limits agree but f(c) is undefined, or f(c) is infinite
The one-sided limits are different finite numbers, or one side is unbounded
questions.concept: Existence criterion for a two-sided limit
questions.why:
A two-sided limit is a single finite number that f approaches from either side. It fails if the sides settle on different heights, which on a graph is a break where the curve restarts at a new level, a jump. It also fails if a side runs off to +∞ or −∞, since the heights never settle on any real number, and the graph then hugs a vertical asymptote. Note that 'limit = ∞' describes a failure, not a value.

The options about f(c) describe continuity failing, not the limit failing, and a corner has a perfectly good limit.

questions.q: A cell of emf 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.40 Ω delivers a current of 2.5 A to a load. What is the terminal voltage of the cell?
questions.concept: Terminal voltage of a real source
questions.why:
On discharge the terminal voltage is the emf minus the drop across the internal resistance: V = ε − Ir = 9.0 − (2.5)(0.40) = 9.0 − 1.0 = 8.0 V.

10.0 V adds Ir instead of subtracting it (that is the charging case); 9.0 V ignores the internal resistance altogether; 8.6 V subtracts r without multiplying by the current.

questions.q: The terminal voltage V of a cell is plotted against the current I it supplies. The points lie on a straight line through (0 A, 6.0 V) and (2.0 A, 5.0 V). What is the internal resistance of the cell?
questions.concept: Internal resistance from a V against I graph
questions.why:
V = ε − Ir is a straight line with intercept ε and gradient −r. Gradient = (5.0 − 6.0)/(2.0 − 0) = −0.50 V/A, so r = −(gradient) = 0.50 Ω. Units check: V/A is Ω.

2.0 Ω is the negative reciprocal of the gradient, which has units of siemens, not ohms; 6.0 Ω reads the intercept, which is the emf in volts; 2.5 Ω is V/I at the second point, the load resistance, not r.

questions.q: Charges of +3.0 nC and −3.0 nC are held 2.0 mm apart. What is the magnitude of the electric dipole moment?
questions.concept: Dipole moment from charge and separation
questions.why:
p = qd, where q is the magnitude of either charge: p = (3.0 × 10⁻⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻³) = 6.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m, directed from −q to +q.

1.2 × 10⁻¹¹ C·m uses 2q, adding the two charges as though the dipole were not neutral; 6.0 × 10⁻⁹ C·m leaves the separation in millimetres; 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ C·m divides q by d instead of multiplying.

questions.q: A dipole has moment p = 4.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m. Taking k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², find the potential at a point on the dipole axis 2.0 cm from the centre, on the +q side.
questions.concept: Potential on the axis of a dipole
questions.why:
On the axis θ = 0, so V = kp cos θ/r² = kp/r² = (9.0 × 10⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻¹²)/(0.020)² = 0.036/(4.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 90 V.

1.8 V forgets to square r (0.036/0.020); 0 V is the value on the equatorial plane, θ = 90°, not on the axis; 4.5 × 10³ V divides by r³, which belongs to the field formula, not the potential.

questions.q: A dipole of moment 5.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m sits in a uniform field of 2.0 × 10⁵ N/C, with p at 30° to E. What is the magnitude of the torque on the dipole?
questions.concept: Torque on a dipole in a uniform field
questions.why:
τ = pE sin θ = (5.0 × 10⁻¹²)(2.0 × 10⁵)(sin 30°) = (1.0 × 10⁻⁶)(0.50) = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ N·m.

8.7 × 10⁻⁷ N·m uses cos 30° instead of sin 30° (cos belongs in the potential energy, not the torque); 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ N·m drops the angle factor entirely, which is the maximum torque at 90°; 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ N·m is a power-of-ten slip.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor has plate area 4.0 × 10⁻² m² and plate separation 0.50 mm, filled with a dielectric of κ = 3.0. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m, find its capacitance.
questions.concept: Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor with a dielectric
questions.why:
C = κε₀A/d = (3.0)(8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(4.0 × 10⁻²)/(0.50 × 10⁻³) = (3.0)(7.08 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 2.12 × 10⁻⁹ F ≈ 2.1 nF (rounded to two significant figures).

0.71 nF is the vacuum value ε₀A/d, forgetting the dielectric; 0.24 nF divides by κ instead of multiplying (a dielectric raises capacitance); 21 nF uses d = 0.050 mm, a power-of-ten slip in the separation.

questions.q: An applied field of 8.0 × 10⁴ V/m is reduced to 2.0 × 10⁴ V/m inside a dielectric slab. What is the electric susceptibility χ_e of the material?
questions.concept: Dielectric constant and susceptibility from field reduction
questions.why:
Inside a dielectric E = E₀/κ, so κ = E₀/E = 8.0 × 10⁴/2.0 × 10⁴ = 4.0. Then χ_e = κ − 1 = 3.0, dimensionless.

4.0 is κ itself, stopping one step early; 0.25 is E/E₀, the reciprocal of κ; 5.0 adds 1 to κ instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: In a superposition calculation on a two-battery circuit, a 9 V ideal battery is being 'zeroed' so that the other battery can act alone. What replaces the 9 V battery in the diagram?
questions.concept: Zeroing an ideal voltage source
questions.why:
A zeroed ideal voltage source holds 0 V across itself whatever current flows, which is exactly what a wire does, so it is replaced by a short circuit.

An open circuit is what replaces a zeroed current source (it passes 0 A at any voltage), the commonest mix-up; a 9 Ω resistor confuses the emf with a resistance; reversing the battery leaves it active, and superposition needs it switched off.

questions.q: A cell of emf 6.0 V and internal resistance 0.30 Ω is connected to a 2.7 Ω resistor. What are the current, the terminal voltage and the power wasted inside the cell?
questions.concept: Current and terminal voltage of a cell driving a load
questions.why:
One loop, so I = ε/(R + r) = 6.0/3.0 = 2.0 A. The terminal voltage is V = ε − Ir = 6.0 − 0.60 = 5.4 V, which checks against IR = 5.4 V. The power wasted inside is P = I²r = (2.0)²(0.30) = 1.2 W.

2.2 A leaves r out of the current; 0.60 V quotes the lost volts Ir as the terminal voltage; 10.8 W is I²R, the power in the load rather than in the cell.

questions.q: A dipole has moment 6.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m. Take k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². What is the field 3.0 cm from its centre on the equatorial plane, and the axial field at the same distance?
options: 2.0 × 10³ N/C antiparallel to p; axial 4.0 × 10³ N/C
2.0 × 10³ N/C parallel to p; axial 4.0 × 10³ N/C
4.0 × 10³ N/C antiparallel to p; axial 2.0 × 10³ N/C
60 N/C antiparallel to p; axial 120 N/C
questions.concept: Equatorial and axial field of a dipole
questions.why:
On the equatorial plane E = kp/r³ = (9.0 × 10⁹)(6.0 × 10⁻¹²)/(0.030)³ = 0.054/2.7 × 10⁻⁵ = 2.0 × 10³ N/C, pointing antiparallel to p, from +q back toward −q. On the axis at the same distance E = 2kp/r³ = 4.0 × 10³ N/C, parallel to p.

'Parallel' is the axial direction, not the equatorial one; the third option swaps axial and equatorial; 60 N/C divides by r², the point-charge power, instead of r³.

questions.q: A 50 pF air capacitor is charged to 200 V and then disconnected from the battery. A slab of dielectric constant κ = 4.0 is slid in to fill the gap. What are the charge, the new capacitance and the new voltage?
questions.concept: Dielectric inserted at constant charge
questions.why:
Before insertion Q = C₀V₀ = (50 × 10⁻¹²)(200) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ C, and with the battery disconnected that charge has nowhere to go, so it is fixed. The capacitance rises to C = κC₀ = 200 pF, so V = Q/C = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸/2.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 50 V, which is V₀/κ.

Holding V at 200 V and letting Q rise to 40 nC is the battery-still-connected case; 12.5 pF divides by κ instead of multiplying.

questions.q: An electric dipole is placed in a uniform electric field at some angle to the field. Why is the net force on it zero while the torque generally is not, and at what orientations does the torque vanish?
options: The two forces differ in size but act along one line; the torque vanishes at 90°
The field acts only on the positive charge, giving one force and one torque; it vanishes at 90°
The forces are equal and opposite along the same line, so force and torque are both zero at every angle
The forces are equal and opposite but act along different lines, forming a couple τ = pE sin θ; it vanishes at 0° and 180°
questions.concept: Force and torque on a dipole in a uniform field
questions.why:
In a uniform field the two charges feel qE along E and qE against it, equal in size and opposite in direction, so the net force is zero. Their lines of action are separated by the dipole's length, however, so they form a couple of moment τ = pE sin θ, which is zero only when sin θ = 0, that is at θ = 0° (stable) or 180° (unstable).

Unequal forces would need a non-uniform field; the field acts on both charges; and θ = 90° is where the torque is largest, not zero.

checks.topic:
Week 4 Algorithm Concepts, taken conceptually.

What an algorithm is as distinct from a computer program. Why the five-step development process puts a high-level algorithm before stepwise refinement. Why representation must supply sequence, selection and repetition.

Then the analysis side. What priori analysis can settle before any code exists, and what only posterior analysis can report. What Big O actually measures, and what it deliberately throws away. Why worst case rather than best case is the figure normally quoted.

Finally the characteristics and design considerations, as claims about cost and failure. What language independence buys. What robustness means beyond correctness. Why a better algorithm rather than more hardware is what delivers scalability in the e-commerce case study.

questions.q: A flowchart runs: Start; sum = 0; count = 0; then a loop: enter n; sum = sum + n; count = count + 1; decision 'Is count < 5?' with YES back to 'enter n' and NO on to 'Print sum'; Stop. The user types 6, 2, 9, 3, 5, 8 in that order. What is printed?
questions.concept: Tracing a counted accumulator loop
questions.why:
Each pass adds one number and raises count by 1. After the fifth number count = 5, so 'count < 5' is false and the loop exits: 6 + 2 + 9 + 3 + 5 = 25. The sixth value, 8, is never read.

33 adds all six typed values, reading past the fifth; 20 stops after four numbers, as if the test happened before the fifth was added; 5 prints count instead of sum.

questions.q:
How many times does the loop body run?

```
i = 1
while i <= 20:
    i = i + 3
```
questions.concept: Counting iterations of a constant-step loop
questions.why:
The body runs once for each value of i that passes the test: i = 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19 all satisfy i ≤ 20, so the body runs 7 times. After the seventh run i = 22, the test fails, and the loop ends.

6 forgets that 19 still passes the test; 8 counts the failed test at i = 22 as a run; 20 assumes a loop to 20 must run 20 times, ignoring the step of 3.

questions.q:
What is printed?

```
big = 0
for n in [-4, -9, -1]:
    if n > big:
        big = n
print(big)
```
questions.concept: Initialising a maximum before the loop
questions.why:
big starts at 0. Every input is negative, so n > big is false on all three passes and big is never replaced. The code prints 0, a value that was never in the list: initialising the maximum to 0 instead of the first input is the error.

−1 is the true maximum, which a correct version (big = first value) would print; −4 assumes the first value is kept as the maximum; −9 is what a reversed comparison n < big would give.

questions.q: Algorithm A takes 1000N steps and algorithm B takes N² steps on an input of size N. At N = 500, which needs fewer steps, and by how many?
questions.concept: Comparing step counts of two growth functions
questions.why:
A: 1000 × 500 = 500 000 steps. B: 500² = 250 000 steps. B needs fewer, by 500 000 − 250 000 = 250 000. N² has the faster growth rate and overtakes 1000N only once N passes 1000, so for N = 500 the quadratic algorithm is still the cheaper one.

'A, by 250 000' assumes the faster-growing function must already be the slower one; 'B, by 500 000' quotes A's total as the gap; 'A, by 499 500' uses N instead of N² for B.

questions.q: A loop's body runs 3 times when n = 8, 4 times when n = 16 and 5 times when n = 32. Which growth rate does this pattern show?
questions.concept: Reading a growth rate from iteration counts
questions.why:
Each time n doubles, the count rises by only 1: 3, 4, 5 are log₂ 8, log₂ 16, log₂ 32. That is the signature of a loop whose variable is multiplied or divided by a constant, O(log n).

O(n) would double the count when n doubles (8, 16, 32 runs); O(n²) would quadruple it; O(1) would give the same count for every n.

questions.q:
What happens when this runs?

```
n = 5
fact = 1
while n > 1:
    fact = fact * n
print(fact)
```
questions.concept: Loop with no update to its control variable
questions.why:
The condition n > 1 depends on n, but nothing inside the loop changes n. It stays at 5, the test is true on every pass, and the loop repeats forever, so print(fact) is never reached.

120 is what you get if the missing line n = n − 1 were present (5 × 4 × 3 × 2); 5 is fact after a single pass; 1 assumes the body is skipped entirely.

questions.q: Step 3 of a written procedure reads: 'Add a suitable amount to the total.' Which characteristic of an algorithm does that step break?
questions.concept: Characteristics of an algorithm
questions.why:
'A suitable amount' can be read in more than one way, so two people following the step would do different things. An algorithm's instructions must be straightforward and clear, which is the unambiguity characteristic.

Finiteness concerns the number of steps being limited and countable, which one vague step does not affect; language independence concerns not depending on a programming language; input concerns having values to process, and the total is such a value.

questions.q: Before writing any code, a designer works out that an algorithm will execute its innermost statement n² times. Which kind of analysis is this?
questions.concept: Priori versus posterior analysis
questions.why:
The reasoning happens before the algorithm is implemented in any programming language and is independent of the language, which is priori analysis.

Posterior analysis is carried out after implementation and measures the space and running time the program actually uses; space complexity concerns memory, not statement counts; average case is a category of time complexity, not a type of analysis.

questions.q:
What does this print?

```python
total = 0
k = 1
while k <= 4:
    total = total + k * k
    k = k + 1
print(total)
```
questions.concept: Tracing an accumulator step by step
questions.why:
The running totals are 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 4 = 5, 5 + 9 = 14 and 14 + 16 = 30. At k = 5 the test k ≤ 4 fails and 30 is printed.

55 runs one pass too many and adds 25; 10 adds k rather than k × k; 16 keeps only the last square instead of accumulating.

questions.q: Numbers are entered one at a time until 0 is entered, and the 0 itself is not counted. Which design prints how many of the entered numbers were negative?
options: Set the counter to 0, read n, then loop while n ≠ 0 testing n < 0, with no further read inside the loop
Read n, then loop while n ≠ 0 setting the counter to 0, testing n < 0 and reading the next n
Set the counter to 0, read n, then loop while n ≠ 0 testing n < 0 and reading the next n at the foot
Set the counter to 0, read n, then loop while n ≥ 0 testing n < 0 and reading the next n at the foot
questions.concept: Writing a sentinel-controlled counting loop
questions.why:
The counter is set once before the loop; the condition tests the sentinel, n ≠ 0; the body adds 1 when n < 0 and then reads the next n so the condition sees a fresh value; the count is printed after the loop. For 4, −3, −7, 8, 0 it prints 2.

With no read inside the body the condition never changes and the loop runs forever. Setting the counter to 0 inside the loop throws the count away on every pass. The condition n ≥ 0 stops at the first negative number, which is exactly the case being counted.

questions.q: Five actions come from a project to find the largest of a set of numbers entered by a user. (a) Ask whether the same algorithm could also find the smallest number. (b) Write three lines: declare and initialise variables; input numbers; determine the maximum and output it. (c) Ask what type of data the user will enter and what result is expected. (d) Notice that the request never fixes how many numbers will be entered. (e) Replace 'input numbers' with a loop that prompts, reads, compares with the current maximum and counts, until a sentinel is entered. In what order do these match the five algorithm development steps?
questions.concept: Ordering the algorithm development steps
questions.why:
Step 1 is the problem description, and (d) is where the description is found to be incomplete. Step 2 is problem analysis, and (c) fixes the starting and ending points. Step 3 is the high-level algorithm, the three main parts in (b). Step 4 is refinement, and (e) adds detail to one of those parts. Step 5 is review, and (a) asks whether the algorithm solves a more general problem.

Putting (c) first analyses a description not yet known to be incomplete; swapping (b) and (e) puts the refined detail before the plan it refines; starting with (a) reviews an algorithm that does not exist.

questions.q: A linear search checks n items one at a time for a target value. How many comparisons does it make in the best case and in the worst case, and why is the worst case the figure usually quoted?
options: 1 and n; the worst case is the most likely input
1 and n/2; the worst case is the average over all inputs
n and n²; the worst case guarantees an upper bound for any input of size n
1 and n; the worst case guarantees an upper bound for any input of size n
questions.concept: Best case versus worst case time complexity
questions.why:
The best case is the target sitting first: 1 comparison. The worst case is the target last or absent: n comparisons. The worst case is the figure quoted because it is a promise that holds for every input of size n, so it can be relied on for planning and for comparing two algorithms.

The worst case is neither the most likely input nor the average; n/2 is the average when the target sits at a random position; n and n² belong to a method that compares every pair rather than scanning once.

checks.topic:
Week 4 of Elementary Mathematics II worked as problems: taking numbers off graphs and out of formulas.

Reading lim as x approaches c from the left, from the right, the two-sided limit, and the value f(c), from a described graph.

Classifying the point as removable, jump or infinite from the pair of one-sided limits.

The algebraic cases the deck uses: lim(x→3) of 2x+1 read off a line of slope 2 and intercept 1; lim(x→1) of (x²−1)/(x−1) by factoring and cancelling; and one-sided limits of |x| and |x|/x at 0.

Then choosing a constant that makes a piecewise function continuous at its joining point.

Also diagnosing wrong routes. In particular, treating the indeterminate form 0/0 as proof that a limit does not exist, and checking a classification against the graph before quoting it.

questions.q: f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x² − 5x + 6). Classify the discontinuities at x = 2 and at x = 3.
questions.concept: Classifying the discontinuities of a rational function
questions.why:
Factor: (x − 2)(x + 2) / ((x − 2)(x − 3)) = (x + 2)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 2. At x = 2 the factor cancels and lim(x→2) f(x) = 4/(−1) = −4, a finite limit with f(2) undefined: removable (a hole at (2, −4)). At x = 3 the reduced denominator is still 0 while the numerator is 5, so the one-sided limits are ±∞: infinite (vertical asymptote).

'Infinite at 2, removable at 3' swaps the two points; 'removable at both' cancels a factor that is not there; 'infinite at both' reads the zeros of the denominator without factoring first.

questions.q: f(x) = kx − 1 for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = x² + 2 for x > 1. Find the value of k that makes f continuous at x = 1.
questions.concept: Choosing a constant to make a piecewise function continuous
questions.why:
Continuity at the join needs the two one-sided limits to agree with f(1). Left (and value): k(1) − 1 = k − 1. Right: 1² + 2 = 3. Set k − 1 = 3, so k = 4. Check: both pieces give 3 at x = 1.

k = 3 forgets the −1 and equates k to 3 directly; k = 2 moves the 1 across with the wrong sign (k + 1 = 3); k = −4 substitutes x = −1 instead of x = 1 into the left piece.

questions.q: h(x) = |x|/x. Find lim(x→0⁻) h(x), lim(x→0⁺) h(x) and lim(x→0) h(x).
questions.concept: One-sided limits of |x|/x at 0
questions.why:
For x < 0, |x| = −x so h(x) = −x/x = −1; for x > 0, |x| = x so h(x) = 1. Hence lim(x→0⁻) h(x) = −1 and lim(x→0⁺) h(x) = 1. The sides disagree, so lim(x→0) h(x) = DNE (a jump at 0, with h(0) undefined).

'1, 1, 1' treats |x| as x on the left; '−1, 1, 0' averages the two sides instead of declaring DNE; '0, 0, 0' confuses h with |x| itself.

questions.q: Find lim(x→3⁻) (x + 2)/(x − 3).
questions.concept: Sign analysis of a one-sided limit at a vertical asymptote
questions.why:
As x → 3⁻ the numerator tends to 5 (positive) while the denominator x − 3 is a small negative number (x is just below 3). Positive over small negative is large negative, so the limit is −∞; the graph plunges down the left side of the asymptote x = 3.

5 stops at the numerator and ignores the denominator; +∞ gets the sign of x − 3 wrong for x just below 3; 0 treats a nonzero number over zero as if it were zero over something.

questions.q: f(x) = x + 1 for x < 0; f(x) = x² for 0 ≤ x < 2; f(x) = 6 − x for x ≥ 2. At which of the points x = 0 and x = 2 is f discontinuous?
questions.concept: Locating the discontinuities of a piecewise function
questions.why:
At x = 0: left limit 0 + 1 = 1, right limit 0² = 0; they differ, so f is discontinuous at 0 (a jump). At x = 2: left limit 2² = 4, right limit 6 − 2 = 4, and f(2) = 6 − 2 = 4; all three agree, so f is continuous at 2.

'x = 2 only' checks 2 with the wrong pieces or misreads 1 = 0; 'both' assumes every join is a break; 'neither' evaluates f(0) = 0 and f(2) = 4 and stops without comparing the sides.

questions.q: On a graph, both branches of a curve run into an open circle at (2, 3), and a solid dot sits at (2, 0). Which single change makes f continuous at x = 2?
questions.concept: Repairing a removable discontinuity
questions.why:
Both sides approach height 3, so lim(x→2) f(x) = 3 exists; the only failure is f(2) = 0 ≠ 3. Moving the dot up to (2, 3) fills the hole and all three conditions hold, so redefine f(2) = 3.

f(2) = 0 is what it already is, and it is off the curve; 1.5 averages the value and the limit, which fixes nothing; 'no single value' would be right for a jump or an asymptote, but here the limit exists.

questions.q: f(x) = |x − 1| + 1/(x + 2). At which x is f discontinuous?
questions.concept: Corner versus asymptote when locating discontinuities
questions.why:
|x − 1| is defined everywhere and has a sharp corner at x = 1, but a corner is not a break: its limit at 1 is 0 = |1 − 1|. The term 1/(x + 2) is undefined at x = −2 and its one-sided limits there are ±∞, a vertical asymptote. So the only discontinuity is at x = −2 (infinite).

'x = 1 only' mistakes the corner for a break and ignores the division by zero; 'both' counts the corner as well; 'nowhere' overlooks that 1/(x + 2) has no value at −2.

questions.q: Which set of readings makes lim(x→c) f(x) exist while f is still discontinuous at c?
questions.concept: Limit exists but continuity fails
questions.why:
The limit exists when both one-sided limits are the same finite number, and continuity then needs that number to equal f(c). Readings 4, 4 with f(c) = 1 give a limit of 4 that does not match the value: the limit exists, continuity fails (removable).

4, 1, 4 has unequal sides, so the limit itself does not exist; 4, 4, 4 satisfies all three conditions, so f is continuous; +∞, 4, 4 has an unbounded side, so the limit does not exist.

questions.q: A vertical dashed line sits at x = −1. To its left the curve climbs upward hugging the line; to its right it plunges downward hugging the line. There is no dot at x = −1. Give lim(x→−1⁻) f(x), lim(x→−1⁺) f(x), lim(x→−1) f(x), f(−1), the type of discontinuity, and whether choosing a value for f(−1) repairs it.
options: +∞, −∞, ∞, f(−1) = ∞; infinite, repairable by setting f(−1) = ∞
+∞, −∞, DNE, undefined; removable, repairable by setting f(−1) = 0
questions.concept: Reading an infinite discontinuity from a graph
questions.why:
Climbing without bound on the left gives lim(x→−1⁻) f(x) = +∞ and plunging on the right gives lim(x→−1⁺) f(x) = −∞. Neither is a real number and they disagree, so lim(x→−1) f(x) is DNE, and with no dot drawn f(−1) is undefined. A vertical asymptote like this is an infinite discontinuity, and no choice of f(−1) can repair it, because repair requires a limit to match and there is none.

Writing the limit as ∞ treats a failure as a value, swapping the signs misreads the two branches, and 'removable' would need both sides to run into the same finite height.

questions.q: f(x) = x² for x < 1; f(x) = ax + b for 1 ≤ x < 3; f(x) = 2x + 1 for x ≥ 3. Find a and b so that f is continuous at both x = 1 and x = 3.
questions.concept: Two constants for continuity at two joins
questions.why:
Matching at x = 1: the left limit is 1² = 1 and the middle piece gives a + b, so a + b = 1. Matching at x = 3: the middle piece gives 3a + b and the right piece gives 2(3) + 1 = 7, so 3a + b = 7. Subtracting the first equation from the second gives 2a = 6, so a = 3 and b = 1 − 3 = −2, and the middle piece is 3x − 2, which checks out as 1 at x = 1 and 7 at x = 3.

b = 2 is a sign slip in the last step, and a = 2 or a = 4 comes from mismatching one of the two joins.

questions.q: f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x < 2, and f(x) = 3x − 2 for x ≥ 2. Give f(2), the left limit and the right limit at x = 2, and say whether f is continuous there.
options: f(2) = 4, left undefined because of 0/0, right 4; not continuous
questions.concept: Continuity at a join where one piece needs factoring
questions.why:
x = 2 belongs to the second piece, so f(2) = 3(2) − 2 = 4 and the function is defined. On the left, substituting straight into (x² − 4)/(x − 2) gives 0/0, so factor: (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2, and the left limit is 4. On the right, lim (3x − 2) = 4 as well, so the two-sided limit is 4 and equals f(2): f is continuous at x = 2.

Calling the left limit undefined mistakes 0/0 for an answer, a left limit of 0 reads the numerator alone, and f(2) = 0 uses the first piece where its condition fails.

questions.q: At x = 4 both branches of a graph run into an open circle at (4, 2), and a solid dot sits at (4, 7). A student calls this a jump discontinuity because the graph jumps from 2 to 7. What is the correct classification, and what was confused?
options: Jump; the student is right, since the heights 2 and 7 differ
Removable; a jump needs the two one-sided limits to differ, but here both are 2
Infinite; a gap of 5 between the curve and the dot is a break of infinite type
Removable; the limit is 7 and the value f(4) = 2
questions.concept: Removable versus jump classification from a graph
questions.why:
The test for a jump compares the left limit with the right limit, not the limit with the value. Here both branches run into the same height, so lim(x→4) f(x) = 2 exists, and the dot at (4, 7) is simply f(4) sitting off the curve. A limit that exists but does not match the function value is the removable case, and redefining f(4) = 2 would close it up.

The last option has the limit and the value swapped, and 'infinite' would need a branch running off without bound.

checks.topic:
Problem-solving hour on the same Week 4 material of General Physics II.

It sets up and executes numerical work on real sources: finding current and terminal voltage from emf, internal resistance and load, with the power balance as a check.

Multi-source resistive networks three ways: by superposition, by nodal analysis with a chosen reference node, and by reduction to a Thevenin or Norton equivalent.

Then electric dipoles. Computing the dipole moment from charge and separation. The far-field potential k p cos theta over r squared. The axial and equatorial field magnitudes and directions. The torque and potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field.

Finally a parallel-plate capacitor problem with a dielectric inserted at fixed charge.

Emphasis throughout is on choosing the right relation, carrying units, and diagnosing the specific wrong routes that give plausible but incorrect numbers.

questions.q: A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω drives a 3.5 Ω load. What power is dissipated in the load?
questions.concept: Power balance in a circuit with a real source
questions.why:
First the current: I = ε/(R + r) = 12/(3.5 + 0.50) = 3.0 A. Then P = I²R = (3.0)²(3.5) = 31.5 W. Check: source supplies εI = 36 W, internal loss I²r = 4.5 W, and 31.5 + 4.5 = 36 W.

36 W is the total power the source delivers, not what the load gets; 4.5 W is the power wasted inside the battery; 41 W uses I = 12/3.5 = 3.43 A, forgetting the internal resistance.

questions.q: A 12 V source through 3.0 Ω and a 6.0 V source through 6.0 Ω both feed node A, which returns to ground through 2.0 Ω. Both sources have their negative terminals grounded. Using superposition, find the current in the 2.0 Ω resistor.
questions.concept: Superposition in a two-source network
questions.why:
12 V alone (6.0 V source shorted): it sees 3.0 + (6.0 ∥ 2.0) = 3.0 + 1.5 = 4.5 Ω, so I = 2.67 A and V_A = 2.67 × 1.5 = 4.0 V, giving 4.0/2.0 = 2.0 A down through the 2.0 Ω. 6.0 V alone (12 V shorted): 6.0 + (3.0 ∥ 2.0) = 7.2 Ω, I = 0.833 A, V_A = 1.0 V, giving 0.50 A, also downward. Same direction, so I = 2.0 + 0.50 = 2.5 A.

2.0 A is the 12 V contribution alone; 1.5 A subtracts the two contributions although both push current the same way; 5.0 A is 12/3 + 6/6, the current with node A shorted to ground, not with the 2.0 Ω in place.

questions.q: A 15 V source through 3.0 Ω and a 5.0 V source through 2.0 Ω both feed node A, negative terminals grounded, with nothing else connected to A. What is the Thevenin voltage between A and ground?
questions.concept: Open-circuit voltage of a two-source node
questions.why:
V_Th is the open-circuit voltage. With no load the current from the 15 V side equals the current into the 5.0 V side: (15 − V)/3.0 = (V − 5.0)/2.0, so 30 − 2V = 3V − 15, 5V = 45, V_Th = 9.0 V. (R_Th would be 3.0 ∥ 2.0 = 1.2 Ω.)

10 V is the plain average of the two emfs, ignoring the unequal resistances; 20 V adds the emfs as if in series; 11 V weights each emf by its own resistance, (15 × 3 + 5 × 2)/5, the wrong way round: the lower-resistance branch pulls V_A toward itself.

questions.q: Node A is fed by a 2.0 A ideal current source (into A), by a 12 V source through a 6.0 Ω resistor, and is joined to ground by a 4.0 Ω resistor. Ground is the reference. Using nodal analysis, find V_A.
questions.concept: Nodal analysis with a current source
questions.why:
KCL at A, currents in = currents out: 2.0 + (12 − V_A)/6.0 = V_A/4.0. Multiply by 12: 24 + 24 − 2V_A = 3V_A, so 5V_A = 48 and V_A = 9.6 V. Check by superposition: current source alone through 6.0 ∥ 4.0 = 2.4 Ω gives 4.8 V; voltage source alone gives 12 × 4/10 = 4.8 V; sum 9.6 V.

4.8 V is one source's contribution only; 12 V assumes the node sits at the source emf as if the 6.0 Ω dropped nothing; 8.0 V is 2.0 A × 4.0 Ω, treating the zeroed voltage-source branch as an open circuit instead of a wire.

questions.q: Charges of ±4.0 nC are 0.50 mm apart. Taking k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², find the potential at a point 4.0 cm from the centre of the dipole, at 60° to the dipole axis.
questions.concept: Dipole potential at an angle to the axis
questions.why:
p = qd = (4.0 × 10⁻⁹)(0.50 × 10⁻³) = 2.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m, and r/d = 80 so the far-field formula applies. V = kp cos θ/r² = (9.0 × 10⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻¹²)(0.50)/(0.040)² = 9.0 × 10⁻³/1.6 × 10⁻³ = 5.6 V (5.625 V to three figures).

11 V drops the cos 60° factor, which is the on-axis value; 9.7 V uses sin 60° instead of cos; 0.23 V forgets to square r.

questions.q: A dipole of moment 3.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m points along +x. Taking k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², what is the field at a point on the axis 1.0 cm from the centre?
questions.concept: Axial field of a dipole with direction
questions.why:
On the axis E = 2kp/r³ = 2(9.0 × 10⁹)(3.0 × 10⁻¹²)/(0.010)³ = 0.054/1.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 5.4 × 10⁴ N/C, and on the axis the field points the same way as p (along +x) on both sides of the dipole.

2.7 × 10⁴ N/C antiparallel is the equatorial result, half the size and reversed; 5.4 × 10⁴ N/C antiparallel has the right size but the equatorial direction; 5.4 × 10² N/C divides by r² instead of r³.

questions.q: A dipole of moment 4.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m sits in a uniform field of 5.0 × 10⁵ N/C, initially aligned with the field. How much work must be done to rotate it until p is at 120° to E?
questions.concept: Work to rotate a dipole in a field
questions.why:
U = −pE cos θ with pE = (4.0 × 10⁻¹²)(5.0 × 10⁵) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ J. At 0°: U = −2.0 × 10⁻⁶ J. At 120°: U = −(2.0 × 10⁻⁶)(−0.50) = +1.0 × 10⁻⁶ J. Work done = ΔU = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ − (−2.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ J.

2.0 × 10⁻⁶ J is pE, the work to reach 90° only; 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ J is the final energy alone, forgetting the starting energy is negative; 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ J is 2pE, the work to reach 180°.

questions.q: A circuit has two batteries and three resistors. A student solves it by superposition, finding each quantity with one battery at a time and adding. Which of these quantities is NOT correctly found by adding the single-source values?
options: Power dissipated in the 5 Ω resistor
Voltage at the node between two resistors
questions.concept: Limits of superposition
questions.why:
Superposition holds for quantities that are linear in the source strengths: branch currents and voltages add. Power P = I²R is quadratic, so (I₁ + I₂)²R ≠ I₁²R + I₂²R; the cross term 2I₁I₂R is lost. Power must be computed from the total current.

The current, the voltage across a resistor and a node voltage are all linear in the sources and superpose correctly.

questions.q: An 18 V source of negligible internal resistance is in series with 6.0 Ω, a 3.0 Ω resistor runs from that junction to ground, and the output terminals are across the 3.0 Ω. What are V_Th, R_Th and the current in a 4.0 Ω load placed across the terminals?
options: V_Th = 18 V, R_Th = 2.0 Ω, I_L = 3.0 A
V_Th = 12 V, R_Th = 2.0 Ω, I_L = 2.0 A
questions.concept: Thevenin equivalent and load current
questions.why:
With the load off, the divider gives V_Th = 18 × 3.0/(6.0 + 3.0) = 6.0 V. Shorting the ideal source puts 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω in parallel at the terminals, so R_Th = 18/9.0 = 2.0 Ω (and I_N = 6.0/2.0 = 3.0 A). The load then carries I = V_Th/(R_Th + R_L) = 6.0/6.0 = 1.0 A.

18 V skips the divider; 9.0 Ω adds the two resistors in series instead of in parallel; 12 V takes the divider across the 6.0 Ω rather than the output resistor.

questions.q: A dipole made of charges ±4.0 nC feels a maximum torque of 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ N·m in a uniform field of 3.0 × 10⁵ N/C. What are the dipole moment, the charge separation, and the torque when p is at 30° to E?
questions.concept: Dipole moment and separation from maximum torque
questions.why:
τ = pE sin θ peaks at sin θ = 1, so p = τ_max/E = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷/3.0 × 10⁵ = 2.0 × 10⁻¹² C·m. Since p = qd, d = 2.0 × 10⁻¹²/4.0 × 10⁻⁹ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.50 mm. At 30°, τ = pE sin 30° = (6.0 × 10⁻⁷)(0.50) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁷ N·m.

0.25 mm divides p by 2q instead of q; 5.2 × 10⁻⁷ N·m uses cos 30°; 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ N·m treats the torque as independent of the angle.

questions.q: A 200 pF capacitor is charged to 50 V and disconnected from the supply. A slab with κ = 2.5 is then inserted to fill the gap. What are the stored energies before and after insertion, and the energy lost?
options: 2.5 × 10⁻⁷ J before; 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ J after; 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ J lost
2.5 × 10⁻⁷ J before; 6.3 × 10⁻⁷ J after; 3.8 × 10⁻⁷ J gained
5.0 × 10⁻⁷ J before; 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ J after; 3.0 × 10⁻⁷ J lost
2.5 × 10⁻⁷ J before; 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ J after; nothing is lost, it is stored in the slab
questions.concept: Energy change when a dielectric is inserted at constant charge
questions.why:
Q = C₀V₀ = (200 × 10⁻¹²)(50) = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ C and is fixed once the supply is off, so U₀ = ½C₀V₀² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁷ J. Afterwards C = κC₀ = 500 pF and V = Q/C = 20 V, giving U = ½QV = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ J, exactly U₀/κ. The difference, 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ J, is the work the field does pulling the slab in.

An energy that rises by κ is the supply-still-connected case; 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ J drops the ½; and the energy really does leave the capacitor rather than sit in the slab.

questions.q: A charged parallel-plate capacitor is disconnected from its battery and a dielectric slab is inserted between the plates. Why does the field between the plates fall and the capacitance rise?
options: The slab conducts charge away from the plates, so Q falls and C = Q/V rises
The slab pushes the plates further apart, so E = V/d falls and C rises
The slab absorbs the field energy, so E falls, and C rises because the energy now sits in the slab
Polarisation puts bound charge on the slab's faces; the opposing field cuts E to E₀/κ, so V falls while Q holds, and C = Q/V rises
questions.concept: Polarisation of a dielectric
questions.why:
The plates' field polarises the slab: charge centres inside each molecule separate slightly (or permanent dipoles line up), leaving bound negative charge on the face next to the positive plate and bound positive charge opposite. That bound charge produces a field opposing the applied one, so the net field falls to E₀/κ, and with Q fixed V = Ed falls by the same factor while C = Q/V rises by κ.

A dielectric is an insulator and carries no charge away; the plate separation does not change; and absorbing energy is not what changes the capacitance.

checks.topic:
Week 4 Algorithm Concepts taken as practice: tracing the lecture's own algorithms by hand and writing them out.

You trace the sum-and-count flowchart to a printed value and a decision count. You work the maximum-of-a-set problem through the five development steps. You write the refined pseudocode using sequence, selection and repetition correctly.

You then apply the Big O loop rules to concrete code fragments: a decrementing loop, a halving loop, nested loops.

Then you diagnose faulty or wasteful solutions: a maximum initialised to zero, selection used where repetition was needed, and an O(n squared) pairwise comparison where one pass would do.

questions.q:
What does this print?

```
total = 0
for i in range(1, 6):
    if i % 2 == 0:
        total = total + i
print(total)
```
questions.concept: Tracing a loop with a selection inside
questions.why:
i runs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The condition keeps only the even values: 2 + 4 = 6.

9 adds the odd values 1 + 3 + 5, the condition reversed; 15 adds every value, ignoring the if; 12 includes 6, reading range(1, 6) as if it reached 6.

questions.q:
Which line completes the loop so that it prints 5?

```
n = 40
steps = 0
while n > 1:
    ____
    steps = steps + 1
print(steps)
```
questions.concept: Completing the update line of a loop
questions.why:
With n = n // 2 the values are 40, 20, 10, 5, 2, 1: five updates before n > 1 fails, so 5 is printed. Halving the variable each pass is the O(log n) pattern.

n = n − 10 gives 40, 30, 20, 10, 0 and prints 4; n = n // 3 gives 40, 13, 4, 1 and prints 3; n = n − 5 takes eight passes to reach 0 and prints 8.

questions.q:
This prints 6. Which single change makes it print 18?

```
for n in [4, 8, 6]:
    total = 0
    total = total + n
print(total)
```
questions.concept: Accumulator reset inside a loop
questions.why:
total is set back to 0 on every pass, so it only ever holds the latest n and ends as 6. Moving total = 0 above the loop lets the sum build: 4, then 12, then 18.

total * n keeps multiplying 0 and prints 0; indenting the print produces three lines 4, 8, 6; print(n) prints the last item, 6.

questions.q:
What does this print?

```
total = 0
count = 0
for n in [5, 8, -1, 7]:
    if n == -1:
        break
    total = total + n
    count = count + 1
print(total, count)
```
questions.concept: Sentinel-controlled loop
questions.why:
5 and 8 are added (total 13, count 2). The third item is the sentinel −1, so break leaves the loop before the sentinel is added or counted, and 7 is never seen. Output: 13 2.

20 3 ignores the sentinel and adds 7; 12 3 adds the sentinel −1 itself and counts it; 13 3 stops the sum but still counts the sentinel.

questions.q: Which pseudocode prints the sum 1 + 2 + … + n for a given n ≥ 1?
options: total = 0; i = 1; while i < n: total = total + i; i = i + 1; print total
total = 0; i = 1; while i ≤ n: total = total + i; print total
total = 0; i = 1; while i ≤ n: total = total + i; i = i + 1; print total
total = 0; i = 0; while i ≤ n: i = i + 1; total = total + i; print total
questions.concept: Choosing the correct loop implementation
questions.why:
The loop must include i = n, add i before moving on, and increase i each pass. For n = 4: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

The i < n version stops before n and prints 6 for n = 4; the version with no i = i + 1 never changes i and never ends; the version starting at i = 0 and incrementing before adding sums 1 to n + 1 and prints 15.

questions.concept: Counting executions of nested and sequential loops
questions.why:
The nested loops execute the inner statement 3 × 4 = 12 times. The separate loop that follows adds 6 more: 12 + 6 = 18.

12 forgets the second loop; 72 multiplies 12 by 6 as if the last loop were nested too; 13 adds the three loop lengths 3 + 4 + 6.

questions.q:
What does this print?

```
i = 10
while i > 0:
    print(i, end=" ")
    i = i - 3
```
questions.concept: Output of a decrementing loop
questions.why:
i is printed before it is reduced: 10, 7, 4, 1 all pass the test i > 0. After 1 is printed i becomes −2, the test fails, and the loop ends. Output: 10 7 4 1.

10 7 4 stops one early, testing the next value before printing the current one; 10 7 4 1 −2 prints once more after the test should have failed; 7 4 1 subtracts before printing.

questions.q: A fragment reads five numbers by writing the line `enter n` on five separate lines. Which representation form should replace those five lines?
questions.concept: Sequence, selection and repetition
questions.why:
The same step is executed several times, and writing it out on separate lines is not sustainable, so a loop (while condition is true, do perform activity) is the right form: repetition.

Selection executes a step only if a condition holds; sequence is the plain step-by-step order the five lines already have; stepwise refinement is a development step, not a representation form.

questions.q: A fragment must read exactly 5 numbers from the user with a loop and print their average. Starting from count = 0 and total = 0, which combination of loop header and print line does that?
options: `while count <= 5:` with `count = count + 1` in the body, and `print(total / 5)` after the loop
`while count < 5:` with `count = count + 1` in the body, and `print(total / 5)` inside the loop
`while count < 4:` with `count = count + 1` in the body, and `print(total / 5)` after the loop
`while count < 5:` with `count = count + 1` in the body, and `print(total / 5)` after the loop
questions.concept: Writing a counted accumulator loop
questions.why:
With count starting at 0, the test count < 5 lets the body run for count = 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, which is exactly 5 reads, and the division happens once after the loop. For 4, 6, 10, 8, 2 the total is 30 and 6.0 is printed.

count <= 5 runs the body 6 times and asks for a sixth number; count < 4 reads only 4 numbers but still divides by 5, printing 5.6 for the same input; printing inside the loop prints five running averages instead of one final figure.

questions.q:
What does this print?

```python
a = 1
b = 1
for k in range(4):
    c = a + b
    a = b
    b = c
    print(c, end=" ")
```
questions.concept: Tracing variable updates in a loop
questions.why:
Pass 1: c = 1 + 1 = 2, then a = 1 and b = 2. Pass 2: c = 1 + 2 = 3, a = 2, b = 3. Pass 3: c = 2 + 3 = 5, a = 3, b = 5. Pass 4: c = 3 + 5 = 8, a = 5, b = 8. The output is 2 3 5 8.

2 4 8 16 comes from updating b before a, so both hold the new value and c doubles each pass; 1 2 3 5 prints the old b instead of c; the five-number list runs one pass too many, since range(4) gives four.

questions.q:
Give the Big O time complexity of each fragment and how many times each loop body runs when n = 16.

```
(i)   i = n
      while i > 0: i = i - 1
(ii)  i = n
      while i > 1: i = i // 2
(iii) for i in range(n):
          for j in range(n): s = s + 1
```
options: O(log n), O(n), O(n²); 4, 16 and 256 runs
O(n), O(log n), O(n²); 16, 4 and 256 runs
O(n), O(log n), O(n²); 16, 4 and 32 runs
questions.concept: Big O of loops by the update rule
questions.why:
(i) changes i by a constant step, so the body runs n times: O(n), and 16 runs at n = 16. (ii) divides i by a constant, so the count is log₂ n: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 is 4 runs, giving O(log n). (iii) nests two loops of n, so the innermost statement runs n × n times: O(n²), and 16 × 16 = 256.

Calling (ii) O(n) ignores the halving; 32 runs for (iii) adds the two loops instead of multiplying them; the remaining option swaps the first two complexities.

questions.q: To find the largest of n numbers, one student compares every number with every other, about n² comparisons. A single pass that keeps the largest value seen so far also works. How many comparisons does that single pass need, and why is one pass enough?
options: n − 1; each number is compared once with the largest of all the numbers before it
n; each number is compared once with the first number in the list
n − 1; each number is compared once with its immediate neighbour
n²/2; every pair is still compared, but only in one direction
questions.concept: One-pass maximum versus pairwise comparison
questions.why:
Set the running maximum to the first number, then compare each of the remaining n − 1 numbers with it and replace it whenever the new number is larger. The running maximum always holds the largest of everything seen so far, so after the last comparison it holds the largest of all n. That is n − 1 comparisons, which is O(n) rather than O(n²).

Comparing against the fixed first number never updates the reference and fails as soon as the first number is not the largest; neighbour comparisons find local order, not the maximum; n²/2 is the pairwise method the single pass replaces.

checks.topic: The four constitutions, the early political parties, and the 1914 amalgamation debate.

questions.q: A Governor consulted widely with Nigerians, renamed the Legislative Council the House of Representatives with 136 members, and made Nigerians ministers without ministries or portfolios. Which constitution is this?
questions.concept: Identifying a constitution from its provisions
questions.why: Wide consultation, the 136-member House of Representatives and ministers without portfolios are the marks of the Macpherson Constitution of 1951. Clifford (1922) was drafted with no local input and had a 45-member council; Richards (1947) also had 45 members and no consultation; Lyttleton (1954) was the work of a Colonial Secretary and introduced the federal system.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Clifford Constitution of 1922 is correct?
options: Lagos and the South were under legislative council law while the North was under proclamation
It introduced regionalism with a House of Assembly in each region
It was drafted after wide consultation with Nigerians
It gave Northern Nigeria strong representation in the council
questions.concept: Clifford Constitution of 1922
questions.why: Under Clifford, Lagos Colony and the Southern Provinces were subject to legislative-council-made laws, whereas the Northern Provinces were under proclamation. Regionalism came with Richards in 1947. Wide consultation was Macpherson's approach in 1951; Clifford's constitution had no local input. Northern Nigeria was not represented at all, which is one of the constitution's main criticisms.

questions.q: A historian argues that trade, wars and shared origin legends already linked North and South long before 1914, so the amalgamation only put on paper what already existed. Which school of thought is this?
options: The amalgamation created a deeply divided nation
The amalgamation merely formalised pre-existing inter-group relations
The amalgamation was a jigsaw puzzle that could never be solved
The amalgamation was the work of Nigerian leaders acting from self-interest
questions.concept: Two schools of thought on the 1914 amalgamation
questions.why: There are two schools of thought on the 1914 amalgamation: one that it merely formalised pre-existing inter-group relations, the other that it created a deeply divided nation. The historian's argument that links already existed is the first school. The jigsaw puzzle is only a metaphor for the diversity brought together, and self-interest is a criticism of the leaders of independent Nigeria, not a school of thought about the amalgamation.

questions.q: Put these parties in the order they were formed: (A) National Council of Nigeria and Cameroon; (B) Nigerian National Democratic Party; (C) Action Group; (D) Nigeria Youth Movement.
questions.concept: Chronology of early political parties
questions.why: NNDP 1923 (B), NYM 1935 (D), NCNC August 1944 (A), Action Group 1951 in Ibadan (C): the order is B, D, A, C. The first option puts the NCNC before the NYM, the second puts the NYM before Macaulay's NNDP, and the third puts the Action Group before the NCNC even though the AG was formed partly to forestall the NCNC's control of the Western Region.

questions.q: The Lyttleton Constitution of 1954 introduced the federal system. What does a federal system mean here?
options: All law-making is done by one central legislative council for the whole country
Power is shared between the central and regional governments, each with its own law-making areas
The regions are governed by proclamation from the Governor
Each region has a House of Assembly with advisory functions only
questions.concept: Definition of the federal system
questions.why: Under the federal system power was shared between the central and regional governments, and the regions and the centre each had jurisdiction in law-making over the areas allocated to them. A single central legislative council for all of Nigeria was the Richards arrangement. Government by proclamation was how the North was ruled under Clifford, and advisory functions only describes Lugard's Nigerian Council of 1914.

questions.q:

The user's computer has Verdana and Arial installed but not Gill Sans. Which font does the browser use for body text?
questions.concept: font-family fallback list
questions.why:
font-family is a prioritised list: the browser tries Gill Sans, finds it missing, and moves to the next entry, Verdana, which is installed, so it stops there.

Gill Sans is not installed; Arial would only be a candidate if the browser reached the generic sans-serif entry, but Verdana is found first; fonts are never blended, one is chosen.
