questions.q: How does CSS Grid differ from Flexbox?
options: Grid lays out rows and columns at once; Flexbox distributes items along one axis
Grid is for text; Flexbox is for images
Grid only works inside a media query; Flexbox works anywhere
Grid positions items with float; Flexbox uses margins
questions.concept: CSS Grid versus Flexbox
questions.why:
CSS Grid is a two-dimensional system with precise control over rows and columns together, suited to magazine-style layouts. Flexbox distributes space and aligns items along a single main axis, with the cross axis for alignment.

Neither is tied to a content type; neither depends on media queries; float and margins are older layout techniques, not what Grid or Flexbox use.

questions.q: What can an inline-block element do that an inline element cannot?
options: Start on a new line and fill the parent's width
Be styled by a class selector
Accept width and height while staying on the same line
questions.concept: inline versus inline-block
questions.why:
inline-block flows in the line like inline content but, unlike inline, accepts an explicit width and height. Block elements are the ones that start on a new line and fill the parent width.

Starting on a new line describes block; holding text and being selectable by class are true of inline elements too.

checks.topic: Paragraph components, transition categories, and the punctuation marks and their jobs.

questions.q: Every sentence in Tobi's paragraph is about exam stress, but the sentences jump from causes to remedies and back again with no linking words and no logical order. Which component does the paragraph satisfy, and which does it fail?
options: One idea at a time; topic sentence
questions.concept: Unity versus coherence in a paragraph
questions.why:
Unity requires a single central theme with every sentence relating to it, which this paragraph has. Coherence requires ideas to be orderly and logically connected by cohesive links such as conjunctions and pronouns, which it lacks.

Reversing the pair confuses the two; the topic sentence and one idea at a time are the other two components, but the scenario says nothing about a missing main-idea sentence or a point carried across paragraphs.

questions.q: 'The bridge was closed for repairs; as a result, traffic on the ring road doubled.' To which category of transition words does 'as a result' belong?
questions.concept: Sorting a transition word into its category
questions.why:
'As a result' sits in the Cause and Effect column with Therefore, Thus, Consequently and Accordingly: the second clause is the effect of the first.

Addition words (Furthermore, Moreover) add a point; Sequence words (First, Next, Finally) order steps; Contrast words (However, Nevertheless) oppose the previous idea.

questions.q: 'The kit contains three items ___ a ruler, a compass and a protractor.' Which punctuation mark belongs in the gap?
questions.concept: Colon versus semicolon
questions.why:
A colon introduces a list, explanation or quotation after a complete statement; here the second half delivers the items the first half announced.

A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses, and 'a ruler, a compass and a protractor' is not a clause; a comma there would run the list into the statement; a hyphen joins compound words.

questions.q: A student writes 'a well known author' and is told a mark is missing between 'well' and 'known'. Which mark, and why?
options: En dash, to mark a range
Em dash, to set off information
Hyphen, to join a compound adjective before a noun
questions.concept: Hyphen versus dashes
questions.why:
A hyphen connects the words of a compound adjective placed before a noun, as in 'well-known author' and 'state-of-the-art technology'.

An en dash indicates a range such as pages 10-15; an em dash sets off or emphasises information in place of parentheses or commas; an apostrophe marks possession or a contraction.

questions.q: Which component of a good paragraph requires that all the advantages of a situation be covered in one paragraph and all the disadvantages in a separate one?
questions.concept: One idea at a time
questions.why:
One idea at a time means a paragraph focuses on one idea exclusively, any point introduced is fully discussed there, and a new paragraph never continues a point: advantages in one paragraph, disadvantages in another.

Unity is about every sentence relating to one theme within a paragraph; coherence is about logical order and cohesive links; the topic sentence is the sentence carrying the main idea.

checks.topic: Verifying Kirchhoff's Current Law: the principle, sign convention, readings and KCL versus KVL.

questions.q: At a node, ammeters read I1 = 1.375 mA and I2 = −0.198 mA for the two currents assumed to enter, and I3 = 1.184 mA for the current leaving. Compute I3 from KCL and its percentage difference from the measured I3.
questions.concept: Computing I3 = I1 + I2 with a negative reading
questions.why:
KCL at the node: I3 = I1 + I2, adding algebraically and keeping the sign of I2: 1.375 + (−0.198) = 1.177 mA. Percentage difference = (computed − measured)/measured × 100 = (1.177 − 1.184)/1.184 × 100 = −0.6 %, close agreement, so KCL holds for this row.

1.573 mA drops the minus sign on I2 and adds the magnitudes, which would wrongly suggest KCL fails by a third; −0.007 % quotes the difference in mA as if it were a percentage; +0.6 % has the sign backwards, since the computed value is below the measured one.

questions.q: Four wires meet at a junction. Ammeters show 2.4 mA and 1.1 mA entering and 0.8 mA leaving. The fourth ammeter is wired to read positive for a current entering the junction. What does it read?
questions.concept: Finding the unknown current at a junction with its sign
questions.why:
Entering positive, leaving negative, algebraic sum zero: 2.4 + 1.1 − 0.8 + I4 = 0, so I4 = −2.7 mA. Total entering is 3.5 mA and only 0.8 mA is accounted for leaving, so 2.7 mA must leave through the fourth wire; an ammeter set to read entering as positive therefore shows −2.7 mA.

+2.7 mA has the magnitude but the wrong sign, since the current leaves; −4.3 mA adds all three readings without regard to direction; +0.5 mA is 2.4 − 1.1 − 0.8, subtracting the 1.1 mA as if it were leaving, and then also forgets that the balancing current must leave.

questions.q:
Readings at one node (I1, I2 entering; I3 leaving), in mA:
E1 = 6 V: 0.640, −0.512, 0.128
E1 = 9 V: 0.820, −0.430, 0.390
E1 = 12 V: 1.000, −0.348, 0.925
E1 = 15 V: 1.180, −0.266, 0.914
In which row does the I3 reading fail the KCL check?
questions.concept: Checking each row against KCL
questions.why:
For each row compute I1 + I2 and compare with I3: 0.640 − 0.512 = 0.128 (matches); 0.820 − 0.430 = 0.390 (matches); 1.000 − 0.348 = 0.652, but I3 was recorded as 0.925; 1.180 − 0.266 = 0.914 (matches). The 12 V row fails, so its I3 reading should be re-taken; 0.925 looks like a misread or mis-typed 0.652.

The 6 V row is not suspect just because I3 is small: 0.128 is exactly I1 + I2. The 9 V and 15 V rows also balance to the last decimal place.

questions.q: A branch of the KCL circuit is a 1.0 kΩ resistor across 9.0 V. An ammeter of internal resistance 50 Ω is inserted in series to measure the branch current. By what percentage is the measured current below the true value?
questions.concept: Ammeter internal resistance as a source of error
questions.why:
Without the meter, I = 9.0/1000 = 9.00 mA. With the meter in series the branch resistance is 1050 Ω, so I = 9.0/1050 = 8.57 mA. Fall = (9.00 − 8.57)/9.00 × 100 = 4.8 %. This loading effect is why ammeters must have as low a resistance as possible.

5.0 % takes the meter resistance as a fraction of the resistor alone, 50/1000, instead of 50/1050; 5.3 % subtracts the meter resistance instead of adding it (9.0/950 = 9.47 mA); 0.43 % quotes the drop in mA as if it were a percentage.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's First Law is applied at a node and his Second Law around a closed loop. Which conservation principle lies behind each?
options: First Law: energy; Second Law: charge
First Law: charge; Second Law: energy
questions.concept: KCL versus KVL and their conservation principles
questions.why:
The Current Law (First Law) says the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero because charge cannot pile up or vanish at a junction: conservation of charge. The Voltage Law (Second Law) says the algebraic sum of emfs and potential drops around any closed loop is zero because a charge carried once round a loop returns with the same energy: conservation of energy.

Swapping them pairs each law with the wrong principle; assigning one principle to both misses that KCL is about current at a point while KVL is about potential around a path.

recapCandidates.topic: The limit of f at c and the value f(c) are two independent readings taken from the same graph, and continuity is the separate claim that they agree. Everything in this week follows from that split: the limit is built only from x ≠ c, so redefining f(c) can repair a hole but can never repair a jump or an asymptote.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students hold the model 'the limit is what you get by plugging c in', and it survives because on every unbroken graph they meet — lines, polynomials, |x| — substitution does give the right answer, so the model is only ever punished at a hole, a jump, or a 0/0.
whyQuestions: Why does the definition of continuity list three conditions instead of simply saying lim(x→c) f(x) = f(c)?
Why is f(c) read from the shaded dot on a graph and never from an open circle, even when the open circle is the height both branches approach?
Why can direct substitution be trusted for lim(x→3) (2x + 1) but not for lim(x→1) (x² − 1)/(x − 1)?
Why can a removable discontinuity be repaired by redefining the function at a single point while a jump discontinuity cannot be repaired at all?
Why does lim(x→3⁺) f(x) = +∞ count as the limit failing to exist, when we have written down an answer for it?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It says that lim(x→c) f(x) is computed from values of f at points other than c, so f(c) can be changed, removed or misplaced without altering the limit — which is exactly why the equality of limit and value has to be imposed as its own condition rather than derived.
It matches each type of discontinuity to the condition it breaks: removable breaks (i) or (iii) with the limit intact, so setting f(c) := L repairs it; jump and infinite break (ii) itself, because L⁻ ≠ L⁺ or a side runs to ±∞, and (ii) is a fact about the branches that no single value can touch.
It carries a concrete instance through: (x²−1)/(x−1) has limit 2 at x = 1 with f(1) undefined, so a hole at (1, 2) that redefinition fills — set against a graph whose branches arrive at 3 and −4, where the limit is DNE and no value of f(2) helps.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Take f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) at x = 1. Step 1: substitute — (1 − 1)/(1 − 1) = 0/0, indeterminate, so substitution decides nothing; it only tells us numerator and denominator share the factor (x − 1). Step 2: factor the numerator as a difference of two squares, x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1). Step 3: cancel, legally, because a limit as x → 1 only uses x ≠ 1, so x − 1 ≠ 0 throughout: f(x) = x + 1 for all x ≠ 1. Step 4: one-sided limits — lim(x→1⁻)(x + 1) = 2 and lim(x→1⁺)(x + 1) = 2; they agree on a finite number, so lim(x→1) f(x) = 2. Step 5: the value — f(1) is still 0/0, undefined, because cancelling changed the formula but never the domain. Step 6: classify — limit exists and is finite, value missing, so a removable discontinuity: the line y = x + 1 with an open circle at (1, 2). Step 7: repair — define F(x) = f(x) for x ≠ 1 and F(1) = 2; now F(1) is defined, the limit exists, and they are equal, so F is continuous at 1. Step 8: the contrast that makes the point — on a graph whose left branch runs into 3 at x = 2 and whose right branch starts from −4, with a shaded dot at (2, 1), we get lim(x→2⁻) = 3, lim(x→2⁺) = −4, so lim(x→2) f(x) = DNE and f(2) = 1. Here step 7 is impossible: 3 ≠ −4 is a statement about the branches, and every candidate value for f(2) leaves it standing.

recapCandidates.topic: Big O does not tell you how long an algorithm takes; it describes the growth rate — how the work changes as the input size n changes. That is why the algorithm with the enormous constant, 1000N, is the better one even though it is a thousand times slower than N squared at N = 1, and why the two only trade places at N = 1000.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students treat a Big O class as a speed label stuck to the algorithm — 'O(n squared) is slow, O(n) is fast' — and the model survives because textbook and exam examples always use inputs large enough that the lower-growth algorithm really is the faster one, so the wrong reasoning keeps producing the right answer.
whyQuestions: Why does Big O describe a growth rate rather than a number of seconds?
Why is 1000N considered the more efficient algorithm when its constant is a thousand times larger than the constant in N squared?
Why does the comparison between 1000N and N squared flip exactly at N = 1000, and what does that tell you about which algorithm to choose for small inputs?
Why can two algorithms that are both O(n) still differ by a factor of ten in the time they actually take?
Why does the course still need posterior analysis at all, once priori analysis has told us the growth rates of every candidate?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
A real explanation says what Big O is a statement about: the number of times the work is done as a function of n, counted from the structure of the algorithm before any code exists, not a measured duration.
It shows the crossover concretely — 1000N beats N squared only once N passes 1000 — and draws the right conclusion: growth rate decides which algorithm wins eventually, and 'eventually' can be a long way off.
It closes the loop by naming the two analyses: priori analysis gives the growth rate and is machine- and language-independent; posterior analysis, after implementation, is the only thing that gives actual space and running time.
recapCandidates.workedExample:
Compare two algorithms for the same problem: A does 1000N steps, B does N squared steps.
N = 1:      A = 1,000        B = 1              -> B wins by 1000x
N = 10:     A = 10,000       B = 100            -> B wins by 100x
N = 100:    A = 100,000      B = 10,000         -> B still wins by 10x
N = 1000:   A = 1,000,000    B = 1,000,000      -> they tie; this is the crossover
N = 10,000: A = 10,000,000   B = 100,000,000    -> A wins by 10x
N = 100,000:A = 100,000,000  B = 10,000,000,000 -> A wins by 100x

Read off the mechanism: multiplying N by 10 multiplies A's work by 10 and B's work by 100. A's cost grows in step with the data; B's grows with the square of it, so every tenfold increase in data costs B a further factor of ten relative to A. Nothing about the constant 1000 can stop that, because the constant is applied once while the extra factor of N compounds — which is exactly what Big O keeps and the constant is exactly what it discards, leaving O(N) for A and O(N squared) for B.

The honest caveat, which is the part students miss: if this system will only ever see N below 1000, B is the right choice and Big O is not the deciding argument. Big O tells you which algorithm survives growth; it is posterior analysis, after implementation, that tells you how many seconds either one takes on your machine today.
